blocks.x: Okay, it's going. Baby, since Joe Oliver isn't around anymore, I thought I'd ask you a few questions about Oliver and his band. At the time you knew him, that you played with him, how did you enjoy working with the band? Well, Bill, as far as the band's concerned, it was a swell band to work with. Everybody knew what they were doing, everybody was set with anything went off, everybody was ready. When did you join the Oliver band? Well, I joined the Oliver band by the year of 1921. I left the Stuckford's line in 20 and Joe Oliver sent for me to come to Frisco and we worked on Marcus Street. At the Jitna Dance Hall. And that's where I come in contact with Joe Oliver. Who else was in the band when you joined? Well, there were Henri Dutre, trombone, with my brother John Clannett and Eddie Garland on bass file. I'm forgetting that. Oh, the piano player was Bill. And we had Dave Jones playing sax. Did he play mellophone ever with the band too or just the sax? No, he didn't play mellophone with the King Alva outfit as with the Fade Marable outfit. How did the band compare with the Fade Marable band? There's no comparison because we had more men in the Fade Marable band. There's more harmony. And, uh, well, quite naturally, you know, in any, any band that, uh, that's an orchestra like that, the more men you got, the better music you got. That's the way I feel. Now, I haven't got to work the same way, hasn't got to be the same way. That's the way I feel. I feel that you have more men, you can bring more harmony out. The man has got the stick completed for the melody. And with the harmony out of the band, that makes a good band, I think. Um, how did the bands compare in their, uh, or the people that, how did, how were they received? That is, the public reception. Oh, the reception of the public was very good. And for which one? You mean, which is best, do you think? Or could you compare? Well, I think, I think that the, comparing the sets of people, I think the people that we had on the boat was a much better set of people. Because they danced. Yeah. And they danced everything. And I'm going to tell you a little something, Bill, about your home. We passed through Hanover, Missouri. I think I told you about that. How nobody danced. Oh, yeah. And then when they, when they, when they, we was almost ready to stop playing. Well, about, we almost knocked, couldn't work about 1130. And, uh, this was about 11 o'clock. People started dancing. And good grace, we couldn't give them enough. It was just dance, dance, dance. We had to make an extra trip out of Hanover. That I will never forget. What'd they do, stand around and listen to the French? They stand around and listen. Did they like it, you think? But just... That I didn't understand. I didn't understand. Why was it, why did they look? But, uh, still, I put two and two together within myself and figured this. But they just wasn't used to dancing by Negroes music. And that made a big difference. People are funny anyway. If they don't, regardless if they know anything is good, but it's not from the type of people, or whom the people that they care to, to dance for, or dance with, or enjoy their music, they don't do it. But I don't think it meant any different. Only, it was just surprising to them to have a Negro band there. And I don't know if there's very much prejudice in Hanover, in Hanover, or St. Joe. I don't know if there's very much prejudice there. But I know they didn't dance. And we had to make an extra trip out of them. Had to make an extra trip. And that St. Joe, I think we had a little trouble in St. Joe, too. Missouri. Because the people that was very slow were dancing there. When they had no trouble in Kirkuk, they flocked right in. Very nice, nice crowd of people. Still, we would look the barn like we was wild or crazy or something. Well, that's big time. And I don't believe the people meant that, but just, it was something new to them, that's all. Yeah. Well, at the Royal Garden with Oliver here in Chicago, did they dance there a good deal? Oh, did they dance? Well, actually, all I had to do was make people continue to dance. We'd be playing a number, we'd go down very soft, and I would use sandpaper. Just like, shh, shh, shh. You really used sandpaper in your hand? We used sandpaper. And people would dance by that sandpaper. Just two pieces together sliding? Yeah, just two pieces. Just sliding. And people would dance by that. That's soft. That's how soft we went. Yeah. And people would dance perhaps half hour like that. Fifteen minutes. Um, to get back to Joe Oliver now, I'd like to find out, nobody tells us much exactly what kind of a fellow he was, even how tall was he? Can you think it's Bill Johnson? Well, oh, he was taller than Bill. Taller than Bill Johnson. So he must be close to six feet, maybe. Just about, I think. And, uh, about five foot and nine, something like that. I know he's a tall man. And he weighed 230 pounds. 230. He's quite a big man. And, uh, he was alright as long as you don't cross him. Yeah. He's like anyone else. If you cross him well then, he's pretty mean. Not particularly, not particularly weight anyone, but he was, he was talking very bad, very rough to you. I never had much trouble with him. Some people did. Um, what about his eating? People have told me he was a big eater. You hear those stories. Is that really true? Yes, Bill. Very true. I tell you, he came over to my house once, and, uh, the wife cooked him. Not particularly him, but she cooked a lot of potatoes, a lot of biscuits. And he, uh, cooked a small, small small-sized dishpan. Full. He, and he come down there eating them all. And he would drink, he drank a, a galvanized, uh, two-gallon bucket. Full of, full of juice. Which was made up as, uh, as, uh, lemonade. Yeah. Was that on the job or at home with the dinner? No, at home. At home with the dinner? What did they drink? Did he drink much liquor? Or beer? Or hard liquor ever? No, not in late years. He didn't drink very much. What do you mean by late years? Now, when you knew him, or? When I first knew him, he used to drink an awful lot. And I used to drink with him. That was back in, back in New Orleans? Yeah, back in New Orleans. He could drink anybody's pint. That's where he drank. And he wouldn't give you any of his, either. If he wanted to drink, he'd buy and drink for himself. That was a pint of whiskey. He would drink that. Drink the whole thing. I used to get next to him sometime. And, and take one drink out of it. That's all he'd let me have. Um, what about, um, on the job, you hear stories about having a big bucket there of lemonade or something, or sugar water and things of that kind. Do you remember? Well, yes, well that was, uh, not all the time. Cause, but he liked plenty of water. Drink plenty of water. And quite naturally he wanted to be something sweet, lemonade or something like that. So, he's a great fellow. Only one thing about him. I'm sorry I didn't do it. I'm sorry today that I didn't go back. He wanted me to play with him. I left him in, uh, in 24. The band busted up. And, uh, he came back in, 34. The place I was working, up on, uh, Michigan in, in 51st. Came in and asked me to join a band. That's when the band was, it was on a truck. Yeah. Going, uh, touring around. Yeah, going from town to town. But he had a bus he had bought. And, uh, he asked me would I join a band. It was a bunch of youngsters. He said, uh, it would be good for the kids' morale if I'd join a band. But I had quit myself. He didn't find me. I had quit myself. And so I just wouldn't take any more chances. Cause I was away, I just let it be that way. Yeah. And then again, I was with my brother. He had to make a living. In regards to Joe, he had to make a living so I stayed with him. Yeah. But that's one mistake that I think I made. I should have gone back to him. I don't think he played very long after that. No, he didn't. He didn't play very long before he died. A couple more years and he faded out. How was his lip when you knew it? Was he powerful? Well, I didn't hear him play. No, I mean in the, when you first joined him, was he, oh yes. Was he unusually loud or, uh? He wasn't unusually loud because he used a mute to mute himself down. Oh my God. And what kind of a mute did he usually use? A metal. Metal mute. Just a little, was it one of those little, uh, ones that looks something like a light bulb? Yeah. A little con mute, people told us. That's right. He didn't use any big, uh, uh, mute that stuck out in front of the horn or a rubber plunger? Did he use that ever? Well, he used that on top of this metal mute. A rubber plunger sometime on top of it. Yeah, sometime, yeah. Uh, I've heard too that he had a sugar can or something. He'd used a tin can. Did he ever use that? Well, in front. To my knowing, I, I, I forgot. I'd rather not say so. Yeah. What about a derby hat? Did he ever? Well, very suddenly he used that. He would use that occasionally. That was something he wanted to have this, this, uh, heavy sound. Yeah. Well, he would use that. Now, while we're talking about hats, can you tell anything about how he was dressed? How did he usually dress? Was he neat or did he, uh? Always very neat to be a big man. Very neat. Very neat. Was it the style to wear a derby in those days or not? I don't even remember. Yes, it was the style. Did he ever wear the derby then? Yeah, cause I had one myself. Yeah, it was style. Mm-hmm. And, uh, well, he's such a big man. He wasn't out of proportion, but just, he, he was so big. Yeah. Um. Looked like he's willing to try a trumpet. He's such a big man and he had a trumpet. He usually used a cornet, I guess, in those days, didn't he? A little... No, not particular. Uh, last, last ten or fifteen years, he used trumpet. Used trumpet. Uh-huh. Uh, what kind of uniforms did the, did the band, or how did you all dress? Say, at the Royal Garden, for instance? We had no uniforms. No uniforms. Only in the wintertime, we'd used tuxedos. Tuxedos. Tuxedos all winter. And the whole band dressed the same, the leader dressed the same as the others. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Exactly. Yeah. Um. Let's see, uh, anything else about, uh, Joe? That is, when he talked, uh, did he talk sort of soft, or was he loud spoken, or what? Did he talk a whole lot, or was he sort of a quiet man? Well, no, he was a man who was, had a joke to say all the time. He was kidding and joking all the time. Uh-huh. And, uh, he wasn't a very loud spoken man. He speak in proportion. He never howled at anybody, nothing like that. And, uh, well, he didn't have too much to say unless there's, uh, something for the band, or something for someone to do. Uh, in proportion. He wasn't a man to talk out of proportion. And, uh, his voice was not a proportion. I thought, to my, to my submission, I thought Joe Oliver was a very fine man. Did he have his family with him when he was here, with his wife here? I think so. I think so. His family was here. His daughter. I think his daughter got married here. Uh, she used to be a friend to my nieces and nephews. I don't, I don't know of her. Yeah. Uh, when the band would start a piece, did he, uh, stomp off, or did he sometimes start playing without the... Sometimes he'd have a pickup of two notes or three notes, or, uh, uh, staccato, staccato part, something like that, and Lloyd would join his, his notes. Sometimes he'd just start out by himself then, without the band? Sometimes, that's right. Uh, when he would call a number, say if you were gonna play, well, all I can think of is Royal Garden Blues, would he, uh, uh, give the title to you, or would he maybe just play a couple notes first, softly, like sometimes they do to tell you the tune? Well, perhaps, perhaps he, perhaps he would, he'd tell you what he's gonna play, and, uh, call the numbers out. They would, numbered like, uh, from, uh, one to one hundred, two hundred, like that, he'd call the number out, and you'd get it that way. And when he'd start off, sometime he'd kick it off, and sometime he'd pick up maybe a two note pickup, a one note pickup. I think that's got one note pickup, isn't it? Yes, yes, a one note pickup. Yeah, I don't remember exactly how it goes. It's either one note pickup, or the trumpet, or the trombone picks it up. Did you all play many requests for people, or did, uh, did you have, say at the Royal Garden did you arrange a whole set before you say we were gonna play about a half a dozen numbers? Did he figure out what they were gonna be, or did he just wait? No, he was just waiting. Now he was just waiting until the time presented itself in the play, and he was picking the stack from, he'd get, I'll tell you, he worked this one to one hundred, maybe, or one to three hundred, whatever he had, in his left drawer, and he would pick out the numbers all the way down, from one to so on. And, uh, sometime he'd go over, so on that set, we'd go back, and repeat. But it was a very seldom way to repeat the number. Very seldom. Well, did you, uh, a lot of the bands in New Orleans, and remember how Bunk's band used to do, they'd play a piece twice. If there had any applause at all, they'd play it over again right away. Did he still do that down there quite a bit? Did you, did Oliver do that much, or ever? Well, yes, he did it sometime. But, uh, perhaps we'd have a, uh, uh, repertoire, a repertoire for the night, and he'd have so many, so many numbers to play. And perhaps, uh, during the encores of those numbers, we didn't go back. Because through the night, we had so many numbers, we'd play them. Not particularly, but we would have those many numbers out. Yeah. Playing encores, sometimes you wouldn't get half of them. According to the encores, you played. He, he had, uh, he conducted the band pretty nice. Mm-hmm. About how long did, uh, did most pieces last? About as long as on the record, that's about three minutes? Or did you play them, maybe five or ten minutes sometimes? Well, that depends. That depends on how it was received, and, uh, maybe if we have enough applause, we'd play it back. Well, that was according to him. Mm-hmm. In other words, according to his mind, too. Yeah. Did you ever play the blues, uh, just, uh, improvised blues very often, or? Very, very, very often. And would that, uh, likely run longer, or shorter than the other numbers, or? None that particular. It was up to Joe what he wanted to do. Yeah. What tempos did you use for blues? Pretty slow or fast? Slow tempos. And sometime we'd speed it up just a little for, just the benefit of it making sound different, or something. Yeah. But all blues are slow tempos, Bill. Yeah, they should be, I know. Well, I don't, I don't, I wouldn't say that, none particular. And since I've known better about blues, it hasn't got to be particularly slow, but, uh, you get more, more into them when you're playing in the school. And that's the way blues supposed to be played anyway. Yeah. Like I see these guys with this rock and roll. That ain't nothing but blues. No, that's right. It's fast. Jumped up blues. They think they got something, but that's all that is. I think we'd play blues about mostly all tempos. You'd play as many waltzes, what's the difference? Did you play many waltzes at the Royal Garden or Dreamland? It was, it was practically a dance hall, see. We'd play a string of, of, of numbers, mix them in, Foxtrot, fast and blues. Do you remember this old waltz, Oh How I Miss You Tonight? Did you play that there? Do you remember Joe playing that? Well, we didn't play that for the dance. That may not have been out much in 1923. This was out. About that time. It was out. Cause I heard later that it was almost like a theme song or something. Yeah. Big hits he made out of it. Tell me something else. You've, in the past, you've told me the seating of the band, how the drums are on one end and the trombone, trumpet and so on, and ends up with the bass on the other. That's right. Did you all sit that way at the Royal Garden and? Yes. All in one line. You weren't, you didn't have like some nowadays they call the front line, put the trumpet and clarinet up and then the drums and bass in back. You didn't do that. Cause it's an unbalance. And you, while you've been on the ones that know that. You take a drum and sit in the middle of your outfit, unless you've got your band built around in a circle, it's not going to balance. And that's why these guys don't get, don't get the right balance of the band. Or you can take it and make it a record. You balance the band, put some over here and some over there and the heavy part of your instruments over that. It don't balance right. I'll tell you one experience where you can think about it. When we was writing in New York at the Stuyvesant. You remember we had a time balancing band on? Yeah. And let you, instrumentation was set right where they didn't balance. After all we had to get in the back of the hall, remember? Yeah. And that two double ceiling, that didn't go. Low ceiling and high ceiling. When you played at the Dreamland or Pekin you also sat always in a straight one long line then, when possible? Yeah, practically. We tried to have everybody on the same roof and on the same level. Yeah. That makes a big difference. The drummer didn't, the drummer didn't get up high on a little platform or anything in the back. No. And the piano was right in the line too then usually? Yeah. Yeah. What did you do about intermissions? Where did you, did the band stay on the stand? No, they would get down and stretch our legs and walk around, go outside, smoke. I've seen the time that it was customary of the band enough to sit on the stand and smoke. You had to get off the stand. How high was the stand at the Royal Garden? Well it was about four feet. Oh, higher, higher than the bed here for instance? Yes. It would be higher. Yeah, they would go up steps. Go up a few steps. And it wasn't too high, it was about, it reached a person's head level. Almost up to the... Yeah, it reached almost to the person's head level. When you were sitting down, you're hip. Yes. For the simple reason, Bill, a lot of people wouldn't understand that. But here's the reason. When your music is up over a person's head, now you may think of this, your music is above a person's head, it's a more even music. When it's up, and then you hit the ceiling and come down, it's not even. Well, what did you think about those real high band stands they have in New Orleans, sometimes up on like balcony, you know, second floor almost? That is still alright because it hits the ceiling, then it comes down from people. Well, if you hear that all over well, it balances itself. The Economin Hall in New Orleans has got that. Yeah, I remember the artesian hall. Yeah, the band sounds like it's way out of town over here. There's a story about that. A lot of people don't know today why that is. Who sticks up the place? That's the way the music sounds. You mean at the Economy Hall, it sounded... Anywhere. Where did it sound out of town? You mean it sounded softer or what? No, it just sounded like it's way away someplace. Sounds too far away. Oh, you mean when the band stand isn't right? Yeah, when it's not right. When it's up too high, or maybe up too low, down too low. Now you can hear a band down low, but you can't way up too high. A lot of musicians don't know that. A lot of leaders don't know that. The next thing, a lot of leaders come in the hall and they just sit anywhere. I don't know if that's what I could. Yeah. You don't pick a place to hear the acoustics of the place, and hear how it sounds, how the bands sound, and the sound better here than they went over here, or sound much better than they do there than over there, all that's in it. And that's what makes a lot of fellas' band don't sound together. That's the reason. It's an instrumentation. I'll tell you a place where we had a lot of trouble. Remember we went to work for Columbia? Was it Columbia? No. Victor. Oh yeah. Remember in New York? Yeah, I remember that street, yeah. You remember all the guy put a bucket of sand, gets some bass drum and mattress and something. Mattress and something like that. You see, that's the reason of that. You have to find out what acoustics of this place to make this band sound out there. So to get back to Joe Oliver now, at the intermission time did he mix with the other fellas, or did he try to sort of stay by himself? Was he just one of the boys, or how did he act? Sometimes. Sometimes he'd have a plan to set, an outfit, then again he would go by himself. Well, I can understand it now. Those days I didn't understand it. Now I understand it. It's like Bunker's just trying to do it. He tried to do the same thing, going by himself. Well, it's a whole lot to that. A lot of people can't have a bunch of men to talk natural with. They feel like any boss man. Yeah. He can't sit and chat with his workers, with his outfit. Get to himself. To me now, it doesn't make any difference. It's just what you talk about. You can't laugh and joke with your coworkers like that, because they'll get so they won't pay attention to you. Yeah. Well, you can't pass jokes with them like one another can. Well, I think of it, what hobbies or what interests, other interests did Joe Oliver have? Did he in sports or what did he do in his spare time? Of course, maybe that's none of our business, but still, I mean, I just wondered if he... That's all right. He was a baseball fiend. Baseball. Oh, he knew every baseball player that ever played. He knew them all. Well, for a fact, the whole band did. Your brother was that way too, wasn't he? Yeah, he was a fan too. Well, what about you? Were you that much of a fan? Not quite. Not until today. I see a player, I don't like him, but that's why he's just another player to me. Yeah. And he may do something good. All right. Somebody else thought he'd do something good too. Now what you gonna do with that guy? Yeah. That's mine. And next thing about it, I feel that it takes nine men to make a ball team. Now regardless of what I can do, I'm more than another body. That's me. Yeah. I feel the same way with the orchestra. It takes seven of us, or nine of us, or six of us to be in that orchestra. Now every man counts. You don't find many fellows said that. No. No. Well, that's where I am. Without those other guys, I can't do nothing. That's the sense. And I can't be no band by myself. That's the sense. And nobody else can. Now regardless of how much he can do, or what solos he does, he still ain't the band. Without that band, you still haven't got nothing. You got to have instrumentation and accordion. I played two piece band. I played three pieces. I played four pieces. I played five pieces. I played eight. I played twelve. I played sixteen. I had played twenty-five. But each one of those people that you got, that I fit, belongs to. Each one of them plays a part. I can't see why one guy can break up a band. He can't. Not if you don't want him to break up. Of course, one man is an awful asset to a band. He can be a soloist. Some of us can play, but they can't be a soloist. You know that to be a fan. Well, about Joe Oliver, was there any other hobbies he had? In New Orleans, they tell about him playing pool quite a bit. Did he do that? Yes, he was a pool player. He loves to play pool. He did up here too, then, in Chicago and San Francisco. Yes, when there were pool rooms. Well, you know in Chicago, we haven't got many pool rooms. No, that's what I know. And guys don't hang around the pool room all day. They'd play cards, something like that, but Joe Oliver wasn't much of a card player. My brother, he'd play cards. But I didn't play much cards, so there wasn't nothing good there. Deutra didn't play cards, so there was nothing doing there. So it's just different things that one can, you can't accomplish these things on a job. On a job that you're lonesome, well, some guy comes and plays some cards, well, then you do it just to do that part of the time away, but you're not fond of it. And the truth about it, Bill, there's a very few sports that I am really fond of. Sounds funny, but I never cared too many for different sports. I like baseball, I like football, I like all sports, but just for me to participate in it, I have to play baseball. This is something you may not know. Yeah, I wonder if you told me. And the batter, John and me, pitch and catcher. Pretty nice. And Johnny was the pitcher. No, he was the catcher. Catcher and you were the pitcher. Yep. But otherwise, my kids get out and play. I used to play pitch and catch when I was a kid, but not as much as you see other kids. Where did you play ball? Here in Chicago then? No, I didn't play ball. I played in New Orleans. On the satellites. Yeah. But my, one of my real hobbies was, a kite. A kite, flying a kite. Flying a kite. That's one of that. And another one was shooting marbles. Mm-hmm. There was a great hand for shooting marbles, and a great hand for flying a kite. And while I used to do other sports of kids, hop, scop, leap frog, and like that. Well, this blues that Richard M. Jones wrote, was it? New Orleans hop, scop, no, Thomas. George W. Thomas. New Orleans hop, scop blues. Was that any special game there, more than other parts? Yes. It wasn't more, but it was a game of kids. Uh, well that's a fellow, a very good friend of mine. I understand he's dead now. George, uh. George Thomas. George Thomas. You knew him. Very well. He's one of my first guys that hired me around, around in the district at that time. Piano and drum. That's where I was through the first time. Where did you work with him? Uh, one of those big houses, I don't remember now which one. One of the big houses, like Lula White's house, it wasn't her house, but similar to that. One in the red light district? Yeah. Wasn't in a place like George, a few clothes or... No, no. Or a cabaret in a house? No. What did you use, drums and piano? Drums and piano. That was all. That was pretty versatile. Yeah. You know you've got to learn that the same as any other thing? Different beats to the drum and piano? It's not easy. Those things, well I had all that to learn when I was coming up. And that's why I was so versatile. I could make a little band two or three people.

Okay, I guess it's going again. We might talk a little bit about Dutre too since he isn't here anymore to talk for himself. No, he was a comical guy. That was a comical man. Really comical. He was really comical. A man could bring a tail to tell you before you get off work, you got a tail to tell you when you get off work. After you get off work, you got one to tell you to keep your company all the way. If you stay out five hours, you got a tail to tell you for five hours. He was a great character. I was for the fun, I was for the laugh. He's a man, he didn't have you laughing. We used to stay together. The man would have me laughing from the time I'd get off the job until the next morning and go into the next morning, he got something for dinner when we get up. The guy had me laughing. He's a man, he likes that joke. He likes to see you laughing. He likes to see you smiling. He wants to see you happy. I never see Dutre once want to see somebody angry. Only one time, Dutre once want to see you laughing. Dutre once want to see you laughing. Dutre once want to see I don't remember how it happened, but he was in the 35th state. And so he and the fellow at the drugstore was Goldberg. So him and this fellow used to kid all the time. It was two brothers. And this one brother, he used to kid all the time with. And so somehow or another, Dutra kidded me so much, and we all laughed so much about it. And this fellow got a gun, belonging to the story, and he shot it. He didn't completely shoot at Dutra or anyone else, just shot, and we all got afraid and run out. But that was the funniest thing. He wasn't shooting at nobody. We all said he was crazy. So when he pulled us, we said, well, you know he's crazy. I'm his own daddy's shop, and he's pulling that kind of business in there. What was his name? I'm trying to think of his name. I know his last name was Goldberg. I can't think of that. In regard to Dutra, how big a fellow was he? Well, he was a 200-pound man, too. Pretty big. Yeah, he weighed about. Was he tall? Well, he wasn't quite as tall. He wasn't quite six foot. But he was about five foot eight. About five foot eight. And he weighed about 175, no, about 180 or 90 pounds. We had no small guys in the band. I was the smallest guy in the band. I was the only little smithy in the band. John weighed 210. Joe Oliver weighed 250. Dutra weighed 190 or 200. I think he weighed 109 pounds. Lil, she's somebody smaller than you. Well, she's a girl. Yeah, I know. But still, before she left the band, she got to be a big girl. She started to get heavy. Got to be a big girl. And Bill Johnson weighed about 190 or 200 pounds. Yeah. And we had quite a healthy band. And you could tell when those guys come at the plane. Louis weighed 2.5 or 2.10. Yeah, but he had them, too. We had no babies. Yeah. Can you tell me something about your music? Did you have arrangements for just about everything you played? Just about. Well, here's the way that happened, Bill. When we come up to making records, then everything was special arranged. Yeah. That's on account of the recording. And everybody, whatever you could say, whatever you could do, you put it in. That's when it was our band. But after the records were made, and they made such a good, big hit, a good hit, a company loved them from that, then it comes to being King Oliver's band. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And that's the way it busted up. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And that's the way it was. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And that's the way it was. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And I would do just as he wished me to do. Yeah. And I'd do like I want, while of course I was all wrong for his idea. And I caught a lot of sand all the time. I was getting balled out every second. And the many rehearsals I made to make records that I didn't make. Because I would make the rehearsal and overnight I'm full of liquor somewhere. And he hated that. And of course. He didn't drink himself then. No, he didn't drink.

Was there ever a time when he was young that he, I know he was always strictly business in the late days, was he ever sort of wild when he was young? No, he never was. Never was. Always was a man to stick to business. Everything he said was low. Was he always a quiet fellow like when I knew him? Well no, he was a joker. He's a big joker too. Yeah. Oh God, he had, he had senses he were. He'd have a joker and he cared, but he's one guy would take it as far as it would go. Take it to the extreme if necessary. And as long as he knew he had a joke, but he'd keep that joke going a long time. And he's a fellow that didn't get disgusted with himself as a joke. But, uh, I have to get so sick of that. And my patients, she's run out very fast. Very fast. But he, he was one of those kinds, he was a long, patient guy. And, uh, which I wasn't. And that made a difference to people. Because he had one way of thinking, I had another way of thinking. But, to pass it all off, I never did get nowhere with mine. I didn't even have to give over to him. It was just, it wasn't nothing. And that was his way. I found a whole lot was wrong with it, but I couldn't dare bring it to other people, because they wouldn't understand. Yeah. Like when you first met us. You thought we were too lovely as a person as a boy. We'd done some recording. Well, I still do. Yeah, but we didn't get lost again. And it wasn't that I did anything, or he did something to me. But we just couldn't see eye to eye. Yeah, I know. A little different type, but I mean, you still got along. Oh, yeah. Like you said, you wouldn't even leave him to go with Joe Oliver. Well, indeed. I mean, you were faithful to him. I wouldn't leave him to go with nobody. I could have got a minute job by myself. And I was the kind that could work with anybody. Of course, he wouldn't believe it. He would believe I was a selfish fellow in the world. But that's what he felt like. Nothing nobody could tell him. It was that, it's that. Did he ever get excited? Did he have a quick temper or anything? Yeah, he had a quick temper. He had a very quick temper. Of course, I had two. One of those kind of things. And oftentimes, we used to fight. But it wasn't the kind of fight that you would think. I get very angry, and he gets very angry. We speak our mind to each other, and double up our fists to fight. Somebody thinks, sure, it's going to be a big fight. But no worth no fight. And for my part, a little while, I'm over it. But he keep it in him all night. All day the next day. If you never make up to him, he'll never make up to you. Well, that's what I didn't like. Well, he's my brother. I knew I had to appreciate him. Because he got all the work. I didn't get any. Oh, you say he was a big baseball fan too. Oh, yeah. What about prize fights? Well, he loved that too. I don't think he'd be throwing the fights the same as the man in the ring. And Houston's out of you got hit. He'd be hitting you. Oh, he'd be hitting you. Every time the guy in the ring hit you. That's right. He's actually going to make the man throw a punch. And he's throwing it right at you. You're going to get it. Actually hit you, huh? Oh, yeah. He hit you. Of course, he was excusing himself. Oh, yeah. Sure. He was cute. Didn't mean it. So wrapped up in the fight. All his emotions. If he was looking at the fight, he'd be in the fight. He'd be as tired as the guy was during the fight. Be tired out after. But I never was that way. I was always emotional, but not that way.

Now I can see what a good guy he was. What type of band do you think he enjoyed working in most? The bigger band or the smaller groups? He worked so many smaller groups. Was that by choice or was it just because they usually only hired three or four? That's all they were hired. Because he knew he could get as much out of the three or four men and he couldn't win five or six. He couldn't get the harmony, but there was work the man got. That's why we got the band of the Hot Seven. And that band put out the work of a band with twelve men. It was the seven. And like the band, he and Louis had the band of five. That Hot Five band put out as much music as ten men would put out. Well, if the man would put somebody else, he wasn't doing anything. He might have somebody that's working and have somebody that's not working. Somebody coming up from him. He was working. Do you remember anything about Johnny's clarinet? What kind he used? Well, I can't know. It was an Albert system, I understand. Do you remember they have what they call improved Albert sometimes? Well, he didn't use improved. An ordinary Albert. The old one, yes. I know that. I know that. Because he and Benny, Benny, Bonnie Bigard talked about that. Because Bonnie used the same kind he did. And then through, through the time change, Bonnie got the new kind and John didn't. And they often talked about it. Do you remember if he ever owned an A clarinet too? Oh yes. That's a B flat. Oh yes, he owned the two of them. He owned the two of them. A and B. Do you remember what kind of reeds he used? Whether they were hard reeds or soft reeds? He used the, I would say the hard reeds. Because the average person couldn't blow his clarinet. He and Bishis used hard reeds. They could blow each other's arms. They would even take it to burn the reed down. Make it stiff. You burn it down to make it stiffen? What did you do? Put a penny over it or a nickel or something like that? Yeah, well that's when they want to burn it off. It got too thin or too soft. They burn that part off. I was seeing them do that many days. Well, they'd take a half a dollar to do it. A half a dollar to get that curve. That's what they'd take. Yeah. Dime couldn't do it, nickel couldn't do it, and a quarter couldn't do it. It had to be a half a dollar. And I don't know, he was a peculiar fellow. He never would make anything tough for anybody. Only when he felt very mean, he'd make it tough for you. He'd get a piece of music and if you didn't like it, well that's a piece of music he's going to play. If it's tough for you, he'd say, well, he's joking, but I didn't send it for you, I sent it for your brother, what you coming with? Who wants to play a piece of music? That kind of a guy. He didn't mean it, but it made things wonderful. But you had to work. You weren't going to skate by or nothing. Oh, one other thing about Johnny and his, they have what they call the double embouchure. Some people put their upper teeth on the clarinet and the lower over, and others put the upper lip on top of their, under their teeth there too. Now wait a minute. Do you remember what she did? That's called the double embouchure. When you put both lips, none of your teeth touch. Or do you think he bit on to the upper part? No, he used his lips. That's why his music doesn't sound so much like staccato. He lifted, he lifted, everything he played he lifted. And he had to cut strong lips too. You think he covered his upper teeth too? The whole mouth. He put on his lips, his lips, done it. All the vibrato was through his lips. Both lips touched rather, you think, rather than the teeth, upper teeth. Now if he did lift teeth, I don't know. How did his teeth, that would be one thing most clarinetists that touch the teeth, their teeth wear. They're like George Lewis's teeth, they're all worn down. Well John didn't wear. He didn't have bad teeth there. Did he have his own teeth until he had them pulled when he was almost sick there at the end, you know? Yes, I think. He had them pulled. For a fact, I think he had them all pulled. The doctor, the doctor suggested that. Until that time he had his own teeth. His own teeth. But the thing about it, I see, now this is very peculiar. I saw the time when John had to have all his teeth extracted and he paid to play. And I saw John Lewis did the same thing. And they both asked the same question to me. It don't sound the same. I said, sure, it sounds fine. And they both had the same number to play. High Society. I think I told you about that, didn't I? No. You didn't mention once those last records that Johnny made were without the teeth. Yeah, it was in 1940. You did say that, yeah. To Decca. And then, this was in, in 40, 45, I made these with Lewis. 45. Yeah. I made those last records with Johnny in 40. And I made these with George Lewis in 45. He didn't have any teeth. So I've experienced men playing kind of without teeth. Same experience. And the both practically asked the same question. Yeah. Well, tell me more, a little bit more about George W. Thomas, if you can remember. What kind of style of piano did he play? Now I tell you. That's a long time ago. I remember that's been in the 14s. That's a long time. Yeah. 40. And here's the point about that. To have the touch and the tone and the way he played for that long time, I can't remember that. You don't remember if he played, well, say something like Jolly Roll Martin or did he play more blues or more ragtime or? Well, he didn't play, I'll say, just blues. He didn't do that. He played all numbers. The, the, the pop number was the same as any other, the George. Yep. Cause he was an entertainer. Did he sing too? Yeah, he sang. And he sang, he was actually a house entertainer. So you know about that he played no blues alone. And I worked with him those years. I just forgot just how it sounds. That was over 40 years ago. Nobody remember that part of it. And I've heard some men write and play on players. Some men write and this and some write and that. I just don't remember that part. Yeah. For a piano player, yes. I wouldn't say it for a band man. I just, I just done forgot. Yeah. But he wasn't real bad or anything like that. No, no, no. He used to read music. I know he composed quite a few pieces. Yeah. So you know, he knew he wasn't a bad guy. Yeah. But sometimes a composer's a good composer, but he can't execute much, you know. Well, he could. He could. He could. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He couldn't play. His wife was a better player than him, I thought. She was very tall too. Yes, I knew him. And she could play a lot of piano. But Richard was one of these kind of fellows that if you didn't know anybody, he'd put something over you. He used to play so and so and so and he never played before in his life. And when you get to play, then you know he didn't play nothing. And he was one of those kind of guys. And they got a whole lot of people like that. They could do this or that and can't do anything. Or he was one of those kind. Or I played that and such and such time. So that didn't get to play and then you'll find he didn't play nothing. You know that. But he was a good player. But you know what I like? Well I guess because I'm from the old school. I actually liked the piano rolls. You know those guys that had something in piano rolls, what you doing here today? That's right, I like them too. And it's just music. Wasn't that that it was doing so much, but it's the way it sounds. I like it myself. I do too. Like it all today. And you know what person, it's kind of wrapped up in music now, I'll send them to that. But she came playing Kay Thompson. She'd be a wonderful musician. At least she did. I sat around about 47, 48, Kay would have been a good musician. Oh did you ever play with piano rolls with your drums? I know in the theater when I was a kid in the picture show they had to play your piano and then they had a colored drummer come there, Doss Taylor they called him. He's dead now, come and play his drums at the piano. No, I never did like that because I know it was false. And I want nothing to do with nothing false. I want it to be a reality or nothing. Yeah, and yet you like to hear the piano rolls. Well not particularly. I like to hear the roll, but not put these drums onto it. Yeah, I know. But I know that was false. Yeah, that's right. I know. Now isn't that peculiar? Yeah. A lot of people just want to hear it anyway. No. I didn't want to hear anything false. I didn't want to hear anything put up. When I was coming along they had these uh, these pianists, upright pianists, to play for theaters. Had the drums and everything onto it. You remember those old pianists? Yeah. Well, people, I see people thought, oh this is the drummer. I just couldn't stand it. Because I know it was false. And I could hear a piece of the violin and everything. It didn't belong to me. Next thing. I was versatile in, in uh, in hearing things. If it wasn't, didn't fit, I would tell you, that don't fit me, man. Yeah. Now a lot of people can't do that. And uh, that's what made me so versatile in drumming. If I would do something myself and it didn't fit right or it didn't fit like I think it should or don't sound good, I wouldn't put it anymore. I wouldn't do it anymore. And of course I got a lot of things in my head to do for drumming. I don't know if I'm versatile enough for it. Now, uh, I'll tell you another thing that you've done for me and I'll thank you for it. I really thank you for it again and again and again. Uh, where you got those tom-toms pulled on those heads. Oh yeah, you like that? Very much, but I haven't been able to use it. Because at that time I was the first. I had no hands and uh, my, my coordination was off so that I couldn't do my hands like I wanted to. Well, I always did say I was going to do it, but I never did go into it. That's why I don't, that's why I don't play uh, uh, type today. You know, my hands was off. Well, um, before our tape is over, could you talk a couple of minutes or so about Jimmy Noon? If you can think of anything about him that might be of interest since he's not here either to tell us. Well, there's not too much I can tell about Jimmy. Jimmy was a quiet one. Oh, he's a quiet one. And you, you didn't know when you were doing good to when you wasn't with Jimmy. He didn't talk much. But, uh, you know anytime he hired you, what's be good for him. He was a good drummer. Or else he don't hire you. He was none of the Johnny Dodds. You're not good for me, I'm not gonna hire. I'm not gonna give you no chance to ruin nobody else. That's where he was. And Jimmy was a nice guy. I actually liked Jimmy. I liked to work for him. And anything you could do, Jimmy would let you do it. Anything you could throw in to make the band sound good or do suit yourself or bring something in that, that's bring you up, you could do it. He never tried to stop from doing anything you could do. Never did. And, uh, believe it or not, I was to go to California with Jimmy. I don't know if you knew that. When was that? In the late years? When he, when he went there. About 1941 or two or something? I know it's been 40. Oh, 40. 1041? Or 40. 1940, I think it was. Brother John died. Now he wanted me to go to California with him. Well, I'm glad I didn't go because that's where he died. Yeah. And I think he died in that same period when he went there. In 1944, I think he died. It was in 1944, well, and I would go time after. Maybe 43 along in there. Yeah. But I'm glad I didn't go because that was going to hit me terrible. It hit me terrible. Yeah, good. Because this had lost John in 40, when I was brand new yet. But that's a lot to work with Jimmy. Well, um, to get back to Johnny, did you ever hear him talk about who his favorite clarinetists were? Yeah. Who did he admire more than anyone? He admired Charlie McCurdy. That was his teacher. That was his teacher. And he loved him. He loved the man more than he didn't. He didn't even like George Barcai much to say Charlie. And, uh, for fact to me, or everybody else that time, he said, left the year, George Barcai played on Charlie. Yeah, he had a big following. But John rather than Charlie. He said, let's see, I think Charlie had a bigger tone than George, too. I think he did. Though his tone was very big for John. I never got to hear him. He never made records. Well, he was a deep tone man. Yeah. For fact, he used to play, he used to play so heavy, he sounded like a bass climber. Really? George, George was something like, I think that's who learned about where he learned from. Big Al-Lower. He said what Big Al-Lower learned from, sea climber. Sea climber. Sea climber. And Johnny never did play a sea, he played a and B. And I think George used to play, George used to play a B, A and B, too. I think McCurdy worked for A and B, but somehow, I know Johnny likes his tone. Mm-hmm. I don't know why. Um, anything about the trumpet players that Johnny used to, which, who was his favorite trumpet player, did he ever say? He worked with a lot of them, Oliver and Louie, and a lot of them in New Orleans, I guess. Did he talk about trumpet players much? No, he, he was the man to, of course he would give you something that you earned, and you had to earn it too. He, you know, and everything that John gives you. He didn't earn it, he wouldn't give it to you. But he used to like Louie, Louie was practice favorite. And, uh, Joe Oliver, well, he figured that Joe, Joe Oliver was the daddy, regardless. Yes. As Joe did wrong, and still Joe Oliver did that. And, uh, he was a man that, he'd give you what belongs to him, but you had to work for it. Better you got nothing from nothing from John. Yeah. John ain't gonna give you nothing for skating or, or pushing over this, pushing over, no sir, you had to work for it. Anytime you got something from John and John gives you the place for it, you worked for it, but you earned it. You get nothing from him. And I'm glad that he was that sort of a little brother to me. Yeah. Because I would, those days I'd go over it. I wouldn't care what, what I did, but he was, I just come right back over there. I ain't gonna let you do that. You gonna do it like anybody else. All right, John. Well, now that's what I want you to do. Do so and so and so. Well, John, I can do it like this. No, you know that's wrong. You know it's wrong yourself. That's why I do it. You better do it right, don't you? And, and, uh, uh, let's call it the same way. Uh, jello roll. No skeet, no jello roll. You done right or else you get down. Yeah. That's where John was. Did John ever have much trouble with the reeds and, I never heard him make a squeak or anything like that. Did he ever have much trouble? If he did, it was so seldom, that there wasn't notes anymore. Never even thought. What about Oliver? Did he ever miss many notes or was he a pretty perfect player? How did he? He's another guy. If he missed it, he blowed it out and you didn't know he missed it. Mm-hmm. He had power. Oh, power. That man could blow a note. He could take any horn brand new and blow it false. Blow it so hard and knock it out of tune. Knock it out of tune. Try like a piece of tin. I seen him do it. Uh, you know where he used to get his horns? He was, well, at Tom Browns. You know where Tom Browns was? He used to be on Lake Street. Oh, up here. Uh, no, west. No, I don't remember that. Well, he, I don't know how Joe found him, but in any way, he found him. Remember what makes he used most of the time? He used to use a york and he used to use, now first he used to use a Holton. He went from Holton to the York. In fact, I think that was the last one of the yorks. Do you remember any make with Johnny's clarinet? Did you get them from, were they French ones or? Yeah, all his, all his songs was French. I guess I imagine Buffet, most of them used Buffet. I don't know. Sometimes Selmer were coming out. No, he had Selmer too. He used Selmer a long, long time. He did? Well, that's a French man. Where did he buy his horns? Did he pick them up secondhand around here sometime? Or get them new? No, he would get them brand new. Because now they don't make them. You have to look around in secondhand stores to find it, Albert, you know. I guess those days you could buy them in a new store. Yeah, it was new. But he had an old one that he, his wife put up with a rubber thing and sitting in the machine. He had an old one that he wouldn't give nothing for. Put the rubber on it and rubber this and rubber that. Who had it? Johnny? Johnny. Yeah. He had to get rid of it, but he eventually had to get rid of it because it wasn't doing no good. Yeah. And after one winter it cracked and it came to leak it while then it would kill him. Yeah. And he had to get rid of it. And Sidney just happened so bad that he had to put one part in his pocket and go around and hold it until he got the other part. And he could play it, regardless of how regular it was. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Well, what is he doing now? Is he playing now? Still in Paris, I guess. Oh, he's back there again. Oh, he's been there all the time. Oh, he's come back to New York and stay there quite a while. He was there for a while, but I think he's been there for a couple of years. That was the time when he had the Cadillac. I don't know. Oh, yeah. Well, you know how long that's been. That's been. Our tape is just about over. Unless there's something else you can think of about Johnny, you think he'd once said or it's... Well, nothing else right now. I think that covers it pretty good, maybe. And that was a great band, wasn't it? All those fellas in all of them, everyone a star. Every guy could work. Every guy was worth something. Every guy was at the back. And every guy giving his part, he's gone. And he didn't make no mistakes. None of them. That's why I would have to be some person. I'm nothing now, Bill, unless I had somebody of that caliber. I had somebody of that caliber, I could have them help to work. I could have them to work. Yeah. But without that, I can't work myself. Mm-hm.

segments.title: Working with King Oliver: band, habits, seating, bandstands and hobbies
segments.summary: Dodds recalls joining Oliver's band in 1921, comparing it to Fate Marable's, and describes Oliver's size, appetite, mutes, dress, call numbers, blues tempos, band seating, bandstand acoustics, hobbies, and early work with George Thomas. This is one indivisible block.

segments.title: Henri Dutrey, the band's weight, and arrangements and records under Oliver
segments.summary: Dodds remembers trombonist Dutrey's humor and a drugstore gun incident, the band members' sizes, and how the band's records were specially arranged until it became King Oliver's band.

segments.title: Johnny Dodds's temper, jokes and fight habits
segments.summary: Dodds describes his brother's joking, patience, quick temper, and how he acted at prize fights, and his loyalty in staying with him.

segments.title: Johnny Dodds's clarinet, plus George Thomas, piano rolls and Jimmy Noone
segments.summary: Dodds discusses Johnny's clarinets, reeds, embouchure, teachers and tooth loss, then George W. Thomas, piano rolls, Jimmy Noone, and Oliver's horns.
